title: Chapter 26 — Some Considerations On War In Democratic Communities
paragraphs: When the principle of equality is developing not just within a single nation but among several neighboring nations at once, as is now the case in Europe, the inhabitants of these different countries — despite their different languages, customs, and laws — nevertheless resemble each other in their equal dread of war and their shared love of peace.*a It is in vain that ambition or anger puts arms in the hands of princes. They are calmed, against their will, by a kind of general apathy and goodwill that makes the sword drop from their grasp, and wars become rarer. As the spread of equality goes on in several countries at once, simultaneously pushing their various inhabitants toward manufactures and commerce, not only do their tastes grow alike but their interests become so mixed and tangled together that no nation can inflict harm on other nations without that harm falling back on itself. In the end all nations regard war as a disaster, almost as severe for the victor as for the vanquished. Thus, on the one hand, it is extremely difficult in democratic ages to draw nations into hostilities. But on the other hand, it is almost impossible for any two of them to go to war without drawing in the rest. The interests of all are so interlaced, their opinions and needs so much alike, that none can remain quiet when the others stir. Wars therefore become rarer, but when they break out they spread over a larger field. Neighboring democratic nations not only grow alike in some respects; they end up resembling each other in almost all.*b This similarity of nations has consequences of great importance for war.

[Footnote a: It is scarcely necessary for me to note that the dread of war shown by the nations of Europe is not solely due to the progress of the principle of equality among them. Apart from this permanent cause, several other accidental causes of great weight could be cited, and first among them the extreme exhaustion left behind by the wars of the Revolution and the Empire.]

[Footnote b: This is not only because these nations share the same social condition; it also arises from the very nature of that social condition, which leads men to imitate and identify with one another. When the members of a community are divided into castes and classes, they not only differ from each other but have no wish or desire to be alike. On the contrary, each tries more and more to keep his own opinions undisturbed, to retain his own distinctive habits, and to remain himself. The characteristics of individuals are very sharply marked. When the state of society among a people is democratic — that is, when there are no longer any castes or classes and all members are roughly equal in education and in property — the human mind moves in the opposite direction. Men are much alike, and they are annoyed, as it were, by any deviation from that likeness. Far from trying to preserve their own distinguishing peculiarities, they try to shake them off so as to identify themselves with the general mass of the people, which is to them the sole representative of right and might. The characteristics of individuals are nearly erased. In the ages of aristocracy even those who are naturally alike strive to create imaginary differences between themselves; in the ages of democracy even those who are not alike seek only to become so and to imitate each other — so strongly is every man's mind carried along by the general impulse of mankind. Something similar may be observed between nations. Two nations sharing the same aristocratic social condition might remain thoroughly distinct and very different, because the spirit of aristocracy is to retain strong individual characteristics. But if two neighboring nations share the same democratic social condition, they cannot fail to adopt similar opinions and manners, because the spirit of democracy tends to assimilate men to one another.]

If I ask why it is that the Helvetic Confederacy made the greatest and most powerful nations of Europe tremble in the fifteenth century, whereas today the power of that country is exactly proportioned to its population, I see that the Swiss have become like all the surrounding communities, and those surrounding communities like the Swiss. So, since numerical strength now forms the only difference between them, victory necessarily goes to the largest army. Thus one of the consequences of the democratic revolution taking place in Europe is to make numerical strength prevail on every field of battle and to compel all small nations either to merge into large states or at least to adopt the policies of the large ones. Since numbers are the decisive cause of victory, every people must of course strive by every means in its power to bring the largest possible number of men into the field. When it was possible to enlist a kind of troops superior to all others, such as the Swiss infantry or the French cavalry of the sixteenth century, it was not thought necessary to raise very large armies. But the case is altered when one soldier is as effective as another.

The same cause that produces this new need also supplies the means of satisfying it; for, as I have already observed, when men are all alike, they are all weak, and the supreme power of the state is naturally much stronger among democratic nations than elsewhere. Thus, while these nations wish to enroll the whole male population in the ranks of the army, they also have the power to do it. The result is that in democratic ages armies seem to grow larger in proportion as the love of war declines. In the same ages, too, the manner of waging war is changed by the same causes. Machiavelli remarks in The Prince "that it is much more difficult to subdue a people led by a prince and his barons than a nation commanded by a prince and his slaves." To avoid offense, let us read "public officials" for "slaves," and this important truth will apply exactly to our own time.

A great aristocratic people cannot either conquer its neighbors or be conquered by them without great difficulty. It cannot conquer them, because all its forces can never be gathered and held together for any long time. It cannot be conquered, because an enemy meets at every step small centers of resistance that check the invasion. War against an aristocracy may be compared to war in a mountainous country: the defeated side has constant opportunities to rally its forces and make a stand in a new position. Exactly the reverse happens among democratic nations. They easily bring their whole available force into the field, and when the nation is wealthy and populous it soon wins. But if it is ever conquered and its territory invaded, it has few resources left. If the enemy takes the capital, the nation is lost. This can be explained easily. Since every member of the community is individually isolated and extremely powerless, no one in the whole body can defend himself or serve as a rallying point for others. Nothing is strong in a democratic country except the state. As the military strength of the state is destroyed by the destruction of the army, and its civil power paralyzed by the capture of the chief city, all that remains is a multitude without strength or government, unable to resist the organized power attacking it. I am aware that this danger may be reduced by the creation of provincial liberties and, consequently, of provincial powers, but this remedy will always be insufficient. After such a catastrophe, not only is the population unable to continue hostilities, but there is reason to fear that it will not even be inclined to try. According to the law of nations accepted in civilized countries, the object of war is not to seize the property of private individuals, but simply to gain political power. The destruction of private property is only occasionally resorted to for the sake of that object. When an aristocratic country is invaded after the defeat of its army, the nobles — who are at the same time the wealthiest members of the community — will continue to defend themselves individually rather than submit. For if the conqueror remains master of the country, he will deprive them of their political power, to which they cling even more than to their property. They therefore prefer fighting to submission, which is to them the greatest of all misfortunes. And they readily carry the people along with them, because the people have long been used to following and obeying them, and moreover have little to risk in the war. Among a nation where equality of conditions prevails, by contrast, each citizen has only a slender share of political power, and often has none at all. On the other hand, all are independent and all have something to lose, so that they are much less afraid of being conquered and much more afraid of war than an aristocratic people. It will always be extremely difficult to persuade a democratic population to take up arms once hostilities have reached its own soil. Hence the necessity of giving such a people the rights and the political character that may impart to every citizen some of those interests that cause the nobles to act for the public welfare in aristocratic countries.

The princes and other leaders of democratic nations should never forget that nothing but the passion and habit of freedom can mount a successful contest against the passion and habit of physical well-being. I cannot imagine anything more prepared for subjection, in case of defeat, than a democratic people without free institutions.

Formerly it was the custom to take the field with a small body of troops, fight in small engagements, and conduct long, regular sieges. Modern tactics consist in fighting decisive battles and, as soon as a line of march is open before the army, rushing on the capital city to end the war at a single stroke. Napoleon, it is said, was the inventor of this new system. But the invention of such a system did not depend on any individual man, whoever he might be. The way in which Napoleon waged war was suggested to him by the state of society in his time. That method was successful because it was admirably suited to that state of society, and because he was the first to use it. Napoleon was the first commander to march at the head of an army from capital to capital, but the road was opened for him by the ruin of feudal society. It may fairly be believed that if that extraordinary man had been born three hundred years earlier, he would not have drawn the same results from his method of warfare — or rather, that he would have had a different method.

I will add only a few words on civil wars, for fear of exhausting the reader's patience. Most of the remarks I have made about foreign wars apply all the more strongly to civil wars. Men living in democracies are not naturally prone to the military character. They sometimes take it on when they have been forced into the field, but to rise as one body and voluntarily expose themselves to the horrors of war — especially civil war — is a course men in democracies are not apt to adopt. Only the most adventurous members of the community agree to run such risks; the bulk of the population stays still. But even if the population were inclined to act, considerable obstacles would stand in its way. It cannot fall back on any old and well-established influence it is willing to obey, no well-known leaders to rally the discontented and to discipline and lead them, no political powers subordinate to the supreme power of the nation that provide effective support to resistance against the government. In democratic countries the moral power of the majority is immense, and the physical resources at its disposal are out of all proportion to whatever physical resources can be brought against it. Therefore the party that occupies the seat of the majority, that speaks in its name and wields its power, triumphs instantly and irresistibly over all private resistance. It does not even give such opposition time to exist, but nips it in the bud. Those who in such nations seek to carry out a revolution by force of arms have no resource but to seize suddenly the whole machine of government as it stands, something better done by a single blow than by a war. For once a regular war begins, the party representing the state is always certain to win. The only case in which a civil war could arise is if the army were to split into two factions, one raising the standard of rebellion, the other remaining loyal. An army forms a small community, very tightly united, endowed with great powers of vitality, and able to meet its own needs for a time. Such a war might be bloody, but it could not be long. Either the rebellious army would win over the government by the sheer display of its resources or by its first victory, and then the war would be over; or the struggle would take place, and then the part of the army not supported by the organized powers of the state would quickly either disband or be destroyed. It may therefore be accepted as a general truth that in ages of equality civil wars will become much rarer and shorter.*c

[Footnote c: It should be remembered that I am speaking here of sovereign and independent democratic nations, not of confederate democracies. In confederacies, since the preponderant power always lies, despite all political fictions, with the state governments and not the federal government, civil wars are in fact nothing but foreign wars in disguise.]
